title: Why Dropshipping Won't Make You Rich (Even With Sales)

beats.text: Dave's store made three thousand dollars in sales. Sounds great, right? Then he checked his bank balance: he was down one thousand five hundred forty six dollars.
He was selling a glowing cat lamp for thirty dollars. Dave never touched the product. A supplier shipped each lamp straight to the customer, and charged him twelve dollars.
At first, the store dashboard looked amazing. Orders were coming in, and Dave thought he'd cracked online business. He hadn't checked what each sale actually cost him.
For every thirty-dollar order, twelve dollars went to the supplier. That left Dave eighteen dollars. So far, so good.
Then the payment company took one dollar and twenty cents. Dave was down to sixteen dollars and eighty cents, and he still hadn't paid for an ad.
Dave bought ads to get people into the store. Each click cost fifty cents. If someone tapped the ad, looked around, and left, Dave still paid.
He got one hundred clicks. At fifty cents each, that was fifty dollars. Only two people bought the lamp, so the ads cost him twenty-five dollars for each customer.
The ad platform took its fifty dollars. The payment company took its fee. The supplier got paid for both lamps. Dave had just sixteen dollars and eighty cents per sale to work with.
Then some lamps arrived late. Customers messaged Dave asking where their orders were. A few wanted refunds, and some disputed the charges with their banks.
Dave pulled out his calculator. He could spend at most sixteen dollars and eighty cents to get one customer and break even, before refunds or any other costs.
But he was spending twenty-five dollars to get a customer. That's at least eight dollars and twenty cents lost on every sale, even before a single refund.
Dave switched off the ads and shut the laptop. Three thousand dollars in sales didn't mean he was making money. He needed to calculate the costs before buying another click.
Follow for money stories with the actual numbers. Next, Dave tries borrowing money to rescue a business that's already losing.
